references.text: Jesus quotes directly from Deuteronomy 6:13, which states that one shall fear the Lord your God, serve him, and swear by his name. In Luke, 'fear' is replaced with 'worship,' but the message of exclusive service to God remains the same.

The prohibition against following other gods expands on the context for Jesus' quote. The verse emphasizes that Israel must not follow other gods, which supports Jesus' rejection of Satan's offer of power in exchange for worship.

Here too, Israel is commanded to fear the Lord your God, serve him, hold fast to him, and swear by his name—a parallel formulation to Deut 6:13 that reinforces the requirement for exclusive worship and service to God alone.

The first commandment forbids having other gods, and the second forbids worshipping idols. Jesus' rejection of Satan is a direct application of these commandments—only the Lord God is to be worshipped and served.
The repetition of the Ten Commandments in Deuteronomy, with the prohibition against other gods and the worship of idols, forms the basis for Jesus' answer to Satan.
Samuel urges Israel to turn their hearts to the Lord and serve him alone, reflecting the same principle that Jesus appeals to: exclusive service and worship of God.

The parallel account in Matthew 4:10 where Jesus answers Satan with the same quote from Deuteronomy: 'You shall worship the Lord your God, and him only shall you serve.' Matthew also includes Jesus' command, 'Away from me, Satan!'
The angel rejects John's attempt to worship him and says that only God is to be worshipped. This reflects the same principle that Jesus emphasizes: worship belongs to God alone.
Again, the angel rejects worship and says, 'Worship God!'—an echo of the exclusive requirement for the worship of God alone that Jesus upholds in the temptation narrative.
Peter rejects Cornelius' attempt to worship him and says that he himself is only a human. The principle is the same: worship belongs to God alone, not to creatures.
